newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tepid outlook for German insurance sales in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Tepid outlook for German insurance sales in 1997.

text.p: German insurers face tepid sales this year as the economic weakness and price pressures that capped 1996 growth continue to weigh on their business, the GDV insurance association said on Monday.

The GDV released preliminary data showing German insurance premiums rose at a post-war low rate of only 2.8 percent to 232.2 billion marks in 1996, after six percent growth in 1995, and that non-life insurance business had no growth at all.

"It's a totally open question whether life insurance can reach or surpass its five percent growth rate of 1996 this year, in view of the government's tax plans," GDV president Bernd Michaels said, referring to Bonn's controversial current proposals to tax certain types of life insurance policy.
And with price pressures still taking their toll on the newly deregulated market, Michaels said non-life policy sales would likely stagnate this year as they did in 1996.
German life insurance sales rose to 92.8 billion marks from 88.4 billion in 1996, while non-life sales remained static at 96 billion marks.

A four percent fall-off in car insurance premiums to 42.5 billion marks, sparked as insurers continued to introduce a range of budget cover deals and rebates, was the main reason for the decline in non-life business.

Germany is experiencing a revolution in motor insurance, with companies scrambling to offer more differentiated pricing, such as discounts for women, infrequent drivers, garage-parkers and certain types of vehicle.
Other smaller branches improved their sales, with loan insurance premiums managing 10 to 12 percent growth, Michaels said.
And earnings generally improved substantially as claims remained modest, costs were stable and companies made more efforts to create profit, the GDV said.

Car insurance results were helped by a decline of 300,000 to nine million in claims instances, despite increased crowding on German roads. However the GDV noted that the size of the average claim had increased sharply.

Turning to the government's proposals to slap a tax on life insurance policies -- a move the insurance industry abhors -- Michaels said German insurers had received thousands of letters from customers worried at the plans, although it was too early to gauge from figures how clients were reacting.

Michaels said he doubted government projections that the tax on life insurance would bring in 3.6 billion marks for state coffers and said he was optimistic that the tax proposal would not go ahead in its current form.
